newsitem.title: UK: Shareholders, GEC hail outgoing Weinstock.
newsitem.headline: Shareholders, GEC hail outgoing Weinstock.

text.p: Lord Arnold Weinstock formally stepped down as chief executive of the General Electric Company Plc on Friday and received a standing ovation from several hundred shareholders gathered at GEC's annual meeting here.
The 72-year-old, who has been the group's driving force and chief strategist for 33 years, responded to the praise of the board and individual shareholders with thanks and a warning.

In his caution, aimed at smaller investors in particular, Weinstock said he was concerned at some of the views that have taken prominence after recent reviews of corporate governance in Britain -- now codified under the Cadbury and Greenbury reports.
He warned investors they should try not to be misled by some of the criticisms of directors and executives that could stem from parts of the codes -- and stick to their own impressions.

"Greenbury and Cadbury are not engraved in stone and brought down from Mount Sinai," he said, adding that he did not like the implications coming from Cadbury that non-executive directors should sometimes be set against executives "as if executives are not to be trusted". One or two points in Greenbury, he added, had created a lever for individuals and institutions to use (in ways that he did not specify) "to persecute directors".

"It's very sad to see," he said. "If you don't trust these (directors), sell your shares. If you do trust them, don't be prepared to believe any innuendo...or let it destroy the trust between shareholders and the people who run your companies."
Weinstock made clear he approved strongly of George Simpson, the man to whom he is handing over his executive duties. Simpson told reporters he will be starting work on Monday morning.

He said he would spend his first year or so getting to know the company, and "stepping into the big man's shoes", and predicted his work would mostly be strategy, "rather than turning things round", as he has done in his previous top jobs.
The meeting heard a long justification of Simpson's generous pay, pensions and bonus package by GEC chairman Lord Prior.

The deal had caused such controversy among fund managers and investors that the performance criteria for the new chief excutive's bonus scheme had to be toughened up in the last few days to ensure it was approved by institutions.
Shareholders at the meeting approved the package by an overwhelming majority with only a handful of objecting votes.
Simpson told reporters later that he felt some more time could have been spent on defining the performance criteria in the first place, and that he was happy about the revisions.
Weinstock, who will continue to work at GEC in an honorary capacity as Chairman Emeritus, will be paid a pension direct from company funds rather than from the GEC pension scheme.
Prior told the meeting that over the years Weinstock had always put off discussing his inclusion in the GEC scheme "because he didn't like the idea of money being spent".
